The study uses a mixed-methods design combining a stratified cross-sectional household survey (n = 475), key informant interviews, six gender-stratified focus group discussions, infrastructure audits, and microbial/physicochemical testing of 91 water points. Among governance and legal-institutional mechanisms, institutional_structure_coordination clearly dominates: the study diagnoses fragmented devolved water governance across national (LOWASCO), county, NGO, and local actors, highlighting overlapping mandates, unclear lines of authority, and ambiguous ownership/mandates over legacy infrastructure that disincentivize rehabilitation and skew spending toward new capital projects (with participation_assistance—weak community involvement and Water Resource Users Associations—analyzed as a secondary theme). All core empirical outcomes—seasonal fetching distance and collection time burden, borehole operational functionality/breakdowns, service reliability, and microbial/chemical potability (E. coli, coliforms, fluoride, TDS/salinity)—belong to effective_access.

Qualitative policy evaluation (in-depth interviews with 10 village/cadre/resident informants, documentation, and field observation) of the Open Defecation Free (ODF) program in Tambak Osowilangun Village, Surabaya. Two governance mechanisms are co-equally central across the effectiveness, efficiency, and supporting/inhibiting factor analyses: participation_assistance (active community participation from planning to monitoring, Great Surabaya Cadre volunteers, community sanitation committees, and NGO counseling/cooperation) and institutional_structure_coordination (municipal policy and dedicated budget allocation, procurement administration, and inter-organizational coordination across the city government, health office, sub-district officials, and NGOs). Outcomes span both primary_connection (household access to proper toilets increasing from ~40% to ~90%) and effective_access (functional sustainability, ongoing toilet maintenance, water availability for sanitation, and sustained utilization vs reversion to open defecation), alongside intermediate administrative procurement delays.

This qualitative socio-historical case study (1990-2022) examines drinking water management in the Bribri Indigenous community of Amubri, Costa Rica, drawing on institutional files, water quality laboratory reports, qualitative interviews, and community workshops. Multiple rule and governance mechanisms are co-equally analyzed to explain service failures: community water committee governance, user participation, Indigenous consultation rules, and state technical/intercultural accompaniment (participation_assistance, primary), Costa Rica's delegated community aqueduct/ASADA model and lack of Indigenous legal personality (regulatory_model_ownership), centralized and intermittent multi-agency state interventions by AyA and the Ministry of Health misaligned with Indigenous territorial governance (institutional_structure_coordination), unsubsidized flat-tariff cost-recovery rules and disputes over tariff levels and metering (fees_tariffs_subsidies), and sanitary orders/inspections (enforcement_sanctions). The central empirical outcome analyzed throughout is effective access—specifically persistent non-potability (fecal coliform contamination), seasonal water availability, and functional sustainability of the aqueduct system.

This mixed-methods household monitoring study (N=17 purposively stratified connected households followed for 180 days from November 2014 to April 2015 in Campina Grande, Brazil) examines how household income (determining domestic tank/cistern storage capacity) and physical hydraulic position in the supply network (topographic elevation and distance from reservoirs) shape the impacts of drought-induced utility water rationing (36-hour weekly scheduled supply suspension) on domestic water storage, per capita consumption, shortage hours, carrying burden, and household hygiene routines. Although background sections briefly mention federal-versus-state water-resource management over the Boqueirão reservoir, the empirical analysis tests socioeconomic and hydraulic-engineering determinants under operational drought rationing rather than any legal or administrative rule-type mechanism from the nine mechanism families (NONE_NO_RULE_MECHANISM). Outcomes center squarely on service continuity/shortage hours, water consumption quantity, domestic storage/water quality, and physical water-carrying burden (effective_access).

The paper is a full-text mixed-methods case study combining quantitative financial modeling and budgetary/balance-sheet analysis (IRR cash-flow projections across the four concession blocks, Siafi-RJ grant allocation tracking, and Cedae operational revenue trends) with qualitative documentary and sociopolitical analysis of concession contracts, legislative committees, and public forums. The central mechanism analyzed is the 2020-2021 PPP/private concession of retail water and sanitation services in the State of Rio de Janeiro under Brazil's 2020 sanitation regulatory framework (regulatory_model_ownership). Secondary mechanisms examined within the concession design include multi-scalar metropolitan governance and fiscal recovery arrangements (institutional_structure_coordination), wholesale water tariff caps/margin-squeeze and grant-revenue diversion away from cross-subsidies (fees_tariffs_subsidies), contractual clauses exempting concessionaires from upgrading informal settlements ('áreas irregulares') lacking prior land-tenure regularization and urban infrastructure (eligibility_status_documentation), and the exclusion of social participation from governance bodies (participation_assistance). Empirically, the study evaluates institutional, fiscal, regulatory, and urban-metropolitan planning governance intermediate outcomes (administrative_outcome)—such as public rent capture, diversion of 67% of state grant proceeds to general payroll/administration, halving of Cedae's operational revenues, and contractual risk-shifting/omissions of metropolitan favelas that create uncertainty around future universalization promises—rather than measuring realized post-concession household connection or service-delivery changes.

This observational study analyzes repeated cross-sectional household WASH surveys (2016, n=1,281; 2017, n=1,360) and household drinking-water testing in opposition-controlled southern Syria using two-sample t-tests and mixed-effects logistic regressions. Empirically, the study tests technical/operational humanitarian Water Safety Plan (WSP) programming (chlorination training, chlorine and tester distribution, chlorination stations, pipe/pump repairs, and volunteer awareness campaigns) alongside physical/behavioral WASH covariates and wartime water-source shifts (piped network vs. private water trucking due to conflict-induced power and infrastructure breakdown), rather than testing any formal legal, regulatory, tariff, or ownership rule (NONE_NO_RULE_MECHANISM; targeted subsidies/vouchers and market regulation are proposed only as policy recommendations in the Discussion). Across the 2016-2017 comparisons, multiple WASH access outcomes are co-centrally evaluated—drinking-water safety (FCR > 0.1 mg/L, the sole WASH outcome modeled as a regression dependent variable), water quantity/continuity/functional sanitation (effective_access), piped network coverage on premises (primary_connection), and household income share spent on water and hygiene affordability (economic_access)—making effective_access the primary outcome family and multiple the multi-outcome label.

This qualitative study (coding of 9 Ugandan national water/decentralization laws and policies alongside 93 semi-structured interviews with political and technical local government officials across 22 sub-counties in 3 districts) examines how regulative, normative, and cultural-cognitive institutions shape local government fulfillment of rural water mandates under Uganda's 2019 National O&M Framework. The central empirical mechanism family is institutional_structure_coordination: the allocation of infrastructure development, contracting, monitoring, and regulatory mandates across decentralized district and sub-county tiers, constrained by centralized intergovernmental fiscal transfers (delayed/insufficient central funding releases) and weak coordination from NGOs and implementers. Delegated management via contracted Area Service Providers replacing community-based management (regulatory_model_ownership) defines the policy shift, alongside secondary themes of informal politician-financed repairs/workarounds (discretion_accommodation), user tariff/enrollment-fee collection and subsidies (fees_tariffs_subsidies), and community sensitization/water user committees (participation_assistance). The primary empirical outcome analyzed is administrative_outcome—specifically, local government actors' compliance with and fulfillment of assigned governance, administrative, regulatory, and service-delivery support mandates (with borehole functional sustainability as the motivating downstream goal rather than a directly measured water-point outcome).

Full-text Spanish comparative descriptive/observational study analyzing official administrative, surveillance, and household survey data (2015-2016) on drinking-water access in Panama and Costa Rica. Mechanistically, the study centrally compares (1) utility/operator models and independent regulator scope (regulatory_model_ownership: national utilities IDAAN/AyA, municipal utilities, public enterprise ESPH, private concessions, and rural community boards JAARs/CS and CAAR/ASADAS in Cuadros 1-3, plus urban-only ASEP regulation in Panama vs nationwide non-municipal ARESEP regulation in Costa Rica), alongside co-equally prominent analysis of (2) regulatory water-quality standard application and compliance surveillance (enforcement_sanctions: Panama's outdated Reglamento Tecnico DGNTI-COPANIT 23-395-99 excluding rural aqueducts vs Costa Rica's universal Decreto Ejecutivo 38924-S and PNMSCSAP Decreto Ejecutivo 33953-S-MINAET) and (3) fragmented sector stewardship and urban/rural mandate splits (institutional_structure_coordination: ASEP vs DISAPAS and weak, fractioned rectoria). Outcomes are co-equally split between household piped network connection coverage (primary_connection: 94.6% vs 97.6% piped supply and Cuadro 4 dwelling tap status) and potable water quality/service quality (effective_access: 74.6% vs 91.8% potable water coverage in Cuadros 2 and 7).

This mixed-methods case study in Quang Ninh Province, Vietnam combines a household survey (n = 270), qualitative in-depth interviews with district officials and utility technical staff (n = 14), and provincial administrative assessments of 262 centralized rural water facilities. Its primary empirical governance exposure is regulatory_model_ownership: Section 4.5 and Table 2 systematically compare government/joint-stock utility corporations, community cooperatives, private enterprises, and village water boards as determinants of system performance, alongside secondary attention to household tariff affordability and subsidy needs (fees_tariffs_subsidies) and urban-rural network integration (institutional_structure_coordination). Across its core objectives and empirical sections, the study evaluates multiple access outcomes: operational continuity, malfunction incidence, drinking-water quality compliance, and functional sustainability (effective_access, the primary overarching outcome), spatial disparities in piped network coverage (primary_connection), and household tariff burden relative to willingness-to-pay thresholds (economic_access).

Boone, Glick, and Sahn (2011) analyze cross-sectional household survey data (2004-2005 EPSPAM, 2,190 households across 73 communities in Madagascar) using a conditional logit model of drinking water source choice (public tap, private tap, well, surface water) and a reduced-form Tobit model of individual hours spent fetching water as functions of physical distance to sources, source availability, household wealth/assets, and demographic characteristics. The study does not evaluate any legal, regulatory, tariff/fee, eligibility, procedural, or institutional rule mechanism (explicitly noting in Note 12 that not even fee information was recorded), warranting NONE_NO_RULE_MECHANISM. The central empirical outcomes concern physical accessibility and water-fetching time burden across water sources, placing the outcome squarely in effective_access, and the cross-sectional econometric survey design is observational.

This observational spatial-ecological study analyzes 1,881 groundwater-supplied drinking water service areas in Arizona over 10- and 20-year periods using geostatistics, clustering, and multivariate regressions. Its central rule-based exposures belong to institutional_structure_coordination: statutory groundwater management boundaries under the 1980 Groundwater Management Act (Active Management Areas vs. Non-Designated Areas) and jurisdictional primacy allocation under the Safe Drinking Water Act (Tribal vs. State oversight). It also compares regulated community water systems against unregulated private domestic well areas (regulatory_model_ownership) and examines SDWA Maximum Contaminant Level compliance/monitoring differences (enforcement_sanctions), though jurisdictional governance and management boundaries clearly dominate. The focal empirical outcomes are groundwater quantity/depletion trends (availability/functional sustainability) and drinking water potability/contamination risk (arsenic and nitrate concentrations, detections, and MCL exceedances), all falling squarely within effective_access.

This study examines community participation in community-based urban sanitation programs in Koja, Jakarta, using surveys (analyzed via exploratory factor analysis, cluster analysis, and binary logistic regression) alongside semi-structured stakeholder interviews, field observations, and educational outreach (mixed_methods). The primary mechanism family is participation_assistance, centered on community collaboration, socialization around drainage and treatment, and participatory community sanitation initiatives, while enforcement_sanctions is secondarily tested via the Sanitation Governance factor (policy enforcement and regular monitoring, which is statistically non-significant in the logistic model). The focal empirical outcome modeled in Hypotheses H1-H8 and Table 4 is citizens' willingness to participate in community-based sanitation programs, which represents an institutional/governance intermediate outcome (administrative_outcome) rather than direct physical connection or household service quality. Confidence is medium because exposures and outcomes are measured through cross-sectional perceptual factor scores and stated willingness to participate rather than evaluation of a specific statutory rule.

This study is a cluster-randomised controlled trial (experimental design) across 332 rural villages (121 clusters) in the Democratic Republic of Congo evaluating the national Healthy Villages and Schools (Villages et Ecoles Assainis, VEA) programme. Among the review's legal/institutional mechanism families, the central rule-type mechanism tested is participation_assistance: the 9-step VEA protocol mandates collective community adoption and action planning, election and training of a village WASH committee, NGO/Health Zone facilitation and assistance, and achievement of seven norms (including a dynamic village WASH committee) for formal certification. Outcomes span multiple co-central families: preregistered primary outcomes measure effective_access (time spent collecting water, quantity of water collected, and use of an improved drinking water source) alongside primary_connection/coverage of improved water and sanitation infrastructure, while secondary outcomes prominently evaluate administrative_outcome (village water governance index, which increased by 1.3 SDs) and economic_access (financial cost of water index). Thus primary_outcome_family is effective_access and assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple is multiple.

Outcomes are co-equally centered on household willingness to pay and affordability relative to service delivery costs (economic_access) and actual household uptake/coverage of safe, formalized fecal sludge emptying to sustain functional on-site sanitation (effective_access), warranting a primary outcome of economic_access and 'multiple' for the multi-outcome label.

This qualitative study (35 semi-structured interviews with London borough staff, TfL, campaigners, delivery drivers, and residents with Crohn's and colitis, plus meeting observation) examines the 'ungoverning' of public sanitation in London. The primary mechanism analyzed is institutional_structure_coordination—specifically central government austerity grant cuts to local authorities, the absence of a statutory mandate requiring local councils to provide public toilets, and fragmented/siloed responsibilities and data across London's 32 boroughs, the GLA, and TfL. Because the study also centrally analyzes the privatisation/sale of municipal facilities and local-authority 'Community Toilet' public-private schemes with commercial businesses (regulatory_model_ownership), alongside private gatekeeper discretion denying workers and non-customers access (discretion_accommodation) and pay-per-use cross-subsidy models (fees_tariffs_subsidies), assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple is 'multiple'. The focal outcome is effective_access: physical availability, opening hours, maintenance quality, disability suitability, and usable access to public toilets across urban space for mobile workers and residents with chronic health conditions.

This mixed-methods case study of four Ethiopian cities (Addis Ababa, Adama, Mekelle, and Dire Dawa) combines key informant interviews and field observations with field hydraulic/chlorine measurements, secondary utility records, demand projections, and ArcGIS/WaterGEMS network simulations. While much of the paper evaluates engineering, hydraulic, and environmental challenges, its empirical institutional and governance analysis (Sections 4.1.8 and 4.2.5) centers on institutional_structure_coordination—specifically incomplete decentralization, local government dependence on regional states, split mandates where local water enterprises supply water while regional water bureaus control project structure and financing, over-centralization, and weak coordination across federal, state, and local water institutions (with secondary discussion of the corporatized 'Enterprise model'/private sector participation and lack of citizen participation). The central access outcomes analyzed are effective_access dimensions: intermittent (non-24/7) supply, volumetric supply-demand deficits, low-pressure nodal delivery shortfalls, residual chlorine and source water quality, and long-term functional sustainability. Confidence is medium because legal/governance rules form one qualitative sub-component of a predominantly engineering-focused assessment.

Although the title references 'Lacking Sanitation Governance' and Section 3.4 briefly mentions national policies as general background recommendations, the empirical analysis tests no legal, regulatory, institutional, or administrative rule mechanism (NONE_NO_RULE_MECHANISM). Using secondary country-level data across 154 countries from GBD 2021 and WHO (2000-2021) combined with BAPC and ARIMA projections to 2030, Comparable Risk Assessment, and decomposition analysis (observational ecological/epidemiological modeling), the study's focal outcome is Deaths Attributable to Unsafe Sanitation in Rural areas (DAUSRs) and age-standardized diarrheal mortality rates—a health/mortality endpoint rather than a household WASH access outcome (NONE_NO_ACCESS_OUTCOME), with rural toilet/sewer coverage proportions modeled via ARIMA as one of the four driving exposure factors of mortality.

This historical-geographical archival study (qualitative design using colonial reports, policy documents, and descriptive historical statistics) examines how early-1900s cholera outbreaks under US colonial rule in the Philippines shaped differential access to potable water and spurred state water infrastructure expansion. Among legal/rule mechanisms, coercive sanitary regulation and policing (enforcement_sanctions)—including armed sanitary inspectors, military policing of the Marikina/Pasig river system to prohibit bathing and domestic use, forced closure of shallow wells, quarantines, and cordons sanitaires—is the most central empirical mechanism analyzed, with secondary attention to costly domestic connection charges under the Carriedo Waterworks (fees_tariffs_subsidies) and state utility/irrigation governance under the Irrigation Act of 1912 and waterworks institutionalization (regulatory_model_ownership). On the outcome side, both water potability/quality, dry-season supply adequacy, and fetching burden (effective_access, the primary focal outcome) and physical infrastructure coverage via urban piped/sewer systems, dams, and provincial artesian wells (primary_connection) are co-equally central (multiple).

This observational (explicitly exploratory and non-causal) quantitative study models data from 1,215 households (Model 1) and 254 functional handpump user groups (Model 2) in Kwale County, Kenya to examine institutional pluralism and uptake of a delegated, performance-based maintenance contract with a professional service provider (FundiFix Ltd). The primary mechanism family is regulatory_model_ownership (comparing community, private/individualist, and public/bureaucratic management models and delegated professional maintenance contracting), while assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple is 'multiple' because the regressions co-equally test fees_tariffs_subsidies (pre-existing regular payment rules, subsidized monthly maintenance tariffs, and fee remissions for vulnerable users—the main statistically significant institutional predictors), participation_assistance (water user committee composition and club rules), and enforcement_sanctions (penalties for non-payment and exclusion for rule violations), alongside broader discussion of devolution (institutional_structure_coordination). Both empirical dependent variables—household 'intent to contract' and user-group 'contract commitment'—are institutional/governance uptake intermediate outcomes (administrative_outcome), whereas reliability, water quality, distance, and cost perceptions enter as explanatory predictors rather than modeled outcomes.

Across both components, two legal/regulatory mechanism families are co-equally central (`multiple`): `fees_tariffs_subsidies` (tiered pricing, billing structures, rate increases, connection fees, lift charges, rebates, and property-tax subsidies, which also feature in ratepayer opposition to costly supply-increase infrastructure) and `enforcement_sanctions` (mandatory water-use requirements, outdoor watering ordinances, fines, enforcement mechanisms, and residential noncompliance), alongside secondary analysis of `review_redress` (tribal, farmer, and environmental litigation) and `institutional_structure_coordination` (interregional/interstate water rights and state-local governance). `fees_tariffs_subsidies` is selected as the single `primary_mechanism_family` because tariff/pricing structures, rate burdens, and rebates span both the demand-reduction and supply-increase conflict analyses as well as the VWCIb index. Confidence is medium because municipal rules serve as the contested/adopted policy portfolio explained by partisan voting (PVI) and hydrology rather than exogenous household-level treatments.

This historical econometric study (244 cities across four Prussian provinces, 1880-1887) tests how local municipal governance and electoral-fiscal institutions—specifically Prussia's tax-weighted Three Class System of town council representation versus equal-vote restricted municipal franchises, interacted with local tax skew—shaped municipal decisions to construct community waterworks networks. Financing, tariff, and special frontage assessment rules (fees_tariffs_subsidies) and cross-national worker wage burdens (economic_access) are examined descriptively to motivate the net-benefit incidence framework, while the primary empirical model is an observational cross-sectional logit analysis (with an instrumental variable for capacity cost) predicting municipal waterworks adoption/network provision (primary_connection).

This observational panel/repeated cross-sectional study analyzes official statistics for 152 decentralized municipal water utilities (si and gun local governments) in South Korea across 2010, 2016, and 2021 using Coulter's coefficient of inequity and Tobit/OLS regressions. On the mechanism side, the central empirical exposures tested in Hypotheses 2-4 are local jurisdictional structure (administrative district tier: city 'si' vs. county 'gun') and decentralized municipal fiscal structure (degree of financial independence and per-capita local tax burden), placing primary_mechanism_family and assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple in institutional_structure_coordination. Utility governance models (private consignment/delegated management and local public enterprise corporatization status, regulatory_model_ownership) are included as non-focal control variables, while municipal water tariff and cost-recovery rules (fees_tariffs_subsidies) are evaluated descriptively for equity adjustments and policy reform. On the outcome side, six water service equity indicators spanning economic_access (average unit water price), primary_connection (water supply coverage rate), effective_access (customer complaints/satisfaction and revenue water ratio), and administrative_outcome (cost-recovery rate and staffing) are analyzed in parallel across all models (assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple = 'multiple'), with average unit price inequity highlighted as the most severe and focal disparity (primary_outcome_family = 'economic_access').

Qualitative ethnographic and interview-based study (26 interviews across 10 households in formal Litha Park and informal Endlovini in Khayelitsha plus 3 City of Cape Town water officials, alongside municipal policy analysis) examining how Cape Town's water governance and Day Zero drought response worsened intra-township water inequality. Multiple legal and administrative mechanisms operate co-equally: (1) fees_tariffs_subsidies (the municipal cost-recovery model, punitive one-size-fits-all water tariffs ignoring multi-household/backyarder yards, and limits of the 6 kL/month means-tested Free Basic Water policy, which anchors the paper's central thesis), (2) eligibility_status_documentation (municipal classification of settlements as formal vs unauthorized/illegal occupation to justify withholding planned services and maintenance), (3) enforcement_sanctions (installation of water management devices overriding indigent FBW protections and disproportionate drought water restrictions/unscheduled cutoffs), (4) participation_assistance (exclusion of informal settlement residents from community leadership and municipal consultative processes), and (5) review_redress (unequal access to municipal maintenance complaint channels tied to formal billing). Outcomes span effective_access (primary: severe supply restrictions below 25 L/person/day, unscheduled water cuts, shared broken/leaking communal standpipes serving ~50 people, and unmaintained burst pipes/sewers), economic_access (exorbitant bills, indigent households forced to pay for leak losses, and tariff pass-through to backyard tenants), and administrative_outcome (differential municipal responsiveness to logged maintenance complaints).

This mixed-methods case study (45 in-depth operator/official interviews, observations/GPS mapping, and n=292 random household surveys in three peri-urban settlements of Dar es Salaam) examines decentralized private self-supply and emerging informal water markets (propertization, commodification, and self-governance by independent self-help and market-oriented operators vs. public utility provision, alongside non-enforcement of commercial groundwater extraction permits under the Water Resources Management Act 2009 and municipal water quality certification, as well as unregulated private connection fees and unit prices).
