Empirically, the study evaluates how these governance arrangements shape both effective_access (reliability, proximity/distance, collection time, and water quality/waterborne illness) and economic_access (unit water prices and household water expenditure exceeding the 5% disposable-income affordability threshold) as co-central outcomes, making effective_access the primary outcome family and multiple the multi-outcome label.

Zhou and Liang (2021) examine how China's household registration system (hukou)—specifically the share of urban temporary residents lacking permanent local legal residency registration—is associated with municipal wastewater treatment capacity and volume of wastewater treated per 10,000 persons (alongside solid waste treatment and public green space). The single focal legal-institutional mechanism empirically tested is legal residency/registration status under the hukou regime (eligibility_status_documentation). For WASH-relevant outcomes, the study measures per-capita wastewater treatment plant capacity (10,000 m3/day per 10,000 persons) and annual quantity of wastewater treated per 10,000 persons, classified as effective_access (sanitation treatment service quantity/capacity per capita, though measured at the aggregate prefecture-city municipal provision level rather than household hookups, creating a secondary conceptual boundary with administrative_outcome). The empirical design uses two-way city and year fixed-effects panel regressions (plus lagged and first-differenced specifications) across 290 Chinese prefecture-level cities from 2008 to 2014 without exploiting an exogenous policy shock (explicitly stopping before the 2014 hukou reform), making it an observational study.

Sohns et al. (2021) conduct a qualitative participatory modeling study using individual interviews and follow-up questionnaires with 14 water policy stakeholders in Alaska to construct individual and merged causal loop diagrams (CLDs) of rural household water vulnerability. Across the economic, infrastructure, and social sub-models and policy themes, multiple governance and legal mechanisms are co-equally examined: intergovernmental fiscal allocation and decentralization (federal/state capital vs. O&M funding splits, state revenue sharing, 1% State Revolving Fund share, and multi-level coordination across decentralized villages; institutional_structure_coordination, the most pervasive structural driver), tariff structures and subsidies (flat monthly vs. volumetric watering-point charges, high-burden rates, and user-fee/O&M subsidies; fees_tariffs_subsidies), stringent water quality and O&M regulatory standards (enforcement_sanctions), competitive grant-writing, operator exam, and permitting barriers (procedural_burden), and utility ownership/regionalized collaborative models (regulatory_model_ownership). The focal problem variable, household water vulnerability, primarily captures effective_access (water quantity, safe quality, fewer non-functional system days, and hauling distance), alongside central co-modeled dimensions of economic_access (household water affordability) and primary_connection (construction of in-home piped water systems versus unserved/haul communities).

This observational cross-sectional study (household survey of n=280 across two semi-arid Rajasthan cities plus NSSO 69th round descriptive statistics, analyzed via chi-square tests and binary logistic regression) examines socio-economic and spatial-institutional determinants of drinking water supply along the urban-rural continuum (city core, outer municipal wards, peri-urban village under Gram Panchayat, and rural village). Among rule/governance dimensions, the central mechanism is institutional_structure_coordination: the urban-rural jurisdictional dichotomy leaves outer fringes and peri-urban villages caught between municipal water governance and rural Gram Panchayat arrangements without institutional piped coverage (with monthly water payment explicitly interpreted by the authors as a proxy for municipal supply vs reliance on informal private tankers rather than a tariff-rule exposure; confidence is medium given the heavy co-emphasis on socio-demographic predictors). For outcomes, the binary dependent variable ('good drinking water supply') co-equally combines physical piped connection within premises (primary_connection) with daily supply continuity, sufficiency, exclusive accessibility, and defect-free water quality (effective_access), warranting effective_access as primary_outcome_family and multiple for assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple.

This qualitative single-site case study examines an NGO-led (CURE) water and sanitation proof-of-concept project in an informal housing cluster in NOIDA, Uttar Pradesh, drawing on CURE project reports and personal observation. Multiple governance mechanisms are co-central: the central thesis evaluates private market-based contracting and community-funded service provision versus public municipal delivery (regulatory_model_ownership), facilitated by NGO-led participatory mobilisation and repeated bureaucratic navigation with local authorities (participation_assistance), necessitated by municipal refusal to provide infrastructure due to illegal settlement status (eligibility_status_documentation) and enabled by non-obstructive street-level official flexibility on solid waste and independently funded works (discretion_accommodation). The primary outcome evaluated is functional sanitation, drainage cleanliness, waste collection reliability, and water quality conditions in the settlement (effective_access).

This qualitative study (based on 30 key-informant interviews alongside parliamentary and Auditor-General reports) examines how Zimbabwe's central government centralized municipal mandates—specifically transferring urban water and sanitation functions to the national parastatal ZINWA via a May 2005 ministerial directive before decentralizing them back in 2009, alongside centralizing vehicle licensing revenue in ZINARA. The dominant mechanism is institutional_structure_coordination (centralization vs. devolution, intergovernmental mandate and revenue allocation, and inter-municipal coordination/billing splits, with secondary discussion of bulk tariffs and bill cancellations under fees_tariffs_subsidies). Empirically, the paper evaluates co-equally central outcomes across effective_access (erratic water supply, severe rationing to two days per week, unpotable water, pipe bursts, deterioration of functional infrastructure, and reliance on unsafe wells) and administrative_outcome (collapse of municipal billing/revenue collection, staffing crises, intergovernmental sabotage, and municipal refusal to recognize ZINWA-approved connections across council boundaries), warranting primary_outcome_family = effective_access and assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple = multiple.

This ethnographic study examines cultural dimensions, interpersonal kin-based sharing networks, risk perceptions, and water-hauling practices shaping household water insecurity in Newtok, Alaska, an unpiped Yupik village. While institutional background factors (e.g., stalled village relocation, unused storage tanks, and a 10-gallon/day school water ration during plant shutdowns) are noted contextually, the author explicitly notes that political-economic and institutional infrastructure processes are not explored in depth, and no legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism is empirically analyzed (`NONE_NO_RULE_MECHANISM`). The primary empirical outcome is `effective_access`, focusing on domestic water quantity (1.91 gal/capita/day of treated water), seasonal supply intermittency when the storage tank runs dry, physical hauling/fetching burdens across treated and natural sources, and perceived water potability/quality. The design is `qualitative`, relying on 6 days of participant observation and semi-structured interviews (n=23) coded in MAXQDA, supplemented only by a descriptive community-wide per-capita consumption figure from monthly water plant logs.

This qualitative study (ethnographic observations, walking/photographic site visits to 22 apartment buildings and one informal settlement, and interviews with officials, experts, middle-class residents, and domestic workers in Mumbai) examines the municipal policy shift and building-level rainwater-harvesting mandates that transfer responsibility for urban water provision from centralized municipal supply (MCGM) to decentralized private/co-operative residential self-provisioning ('localised privatisation', coded under regulatory_model_ownership, with secondary discussion of plot-size thresholds and tenure insecurity in informal settlements under eligibility_status_documentation). The primary empirical outcomes analyzed across the three case studies are effective_access dimensions: 24-hour supply continuity, resilience to shortages, water quantity for domestic/sanitation tasks, perceived potability/water quality, and gendered water-fetching drudgery.

This qualitative study (using desktop review and semistructured interviews with 15 public/water officials and 49 residents across five Cameroonian municipalities, coded thematically with descriptive frequency tables) centrally examines the privatization/restructuring of urban water management—specifically the dissolution of state monopoly SNEC and the public-private lease arrangement splitting infrastructure and service delivery between parastatal CamWater and private operator CDE, alongside proposed PPP alternatives (`regulatory_model_ownership`). Secondary governance discussions address full-cost-recovery pricing and lack of income-stratified tariffs (`fees_tariffs_subsidies`), overlapping ministerial mandates and municipal council exclusion under decentralization (`institutional_structure_coordination`), and an NGO lawsuit over billing without supply (`review_redress`), but `regulatory_model_ownership` clearly dominates as the primary exposure. Empirically, the study co-equally evaluates multiple access dimensions (`multiple`), led by `effective_access` (service irregularity, rationing, multi-month shortages, reliance on polluted streams/wells, and distance to sources) alongside `primary_connection` (low piped network coverage in peri-urban neighborhoods) and `economic_access` (high bills and retail water prices).

This mixed-methods study combines a stratified random survey of 520 households across high- and low-income neighborhoods in Accra, 20 key-stakeholder interviews, focus group discussions, field observations, municipal expenditure records, and GIS spatial mapping of cholera cases. Multiple legal and governance mechanisms are co-central to explaining disparities in water and sanitation access (`assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple` = 'multiple'): (1) `eligibility_status_documentation` (the primary utility/municipal exclusion rule: Ghana Water Company refuses to connect households lacking secure land tenure due to eviction/cost-recovery risk, and municipal authorities exclude 'illegal' settlements like Agbogbloshie for fear of legitimizing tenure), (2) `fees_tariffs_subsidies` (pay-as-you-go water standpipe and public toilet fees, cost-recovery constraints, and AMA's failed 2010 tiered fee-based waste registration scheme), (3) `enforcement_sanctions` (the High Court ban outlawing pan latrines—which drove clandestine night-soil dumping into drains—and the 'one house, one toilet' mandate), and (4) `institutional_structure_coordination` (decentralization without fiscal transfers and shortfalls between planned and actual municipal sanitation expenditure). On outcomes (`assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple` = 'multiple'), the survey primarily tabulates household piped-water and in-house toilet coverage (`primary_connection`, Table 1 and Fig. 3) alongside co-central assessments of service continuity, water contamination, and public toilet condition/distance (`effective_access`), household water/sanitation affordability (`economic_access`), and municipal budget execution (`administrative_outcome`), linking these deficits to cholera incidence.

This quasi-experimental impact evaluation uses propensity score matching (PSM), hurdle models, and instrumental-variable regressions to assess two Indonesian central-to-local intergovernmental performance grant pilots (DAK Reimbursement/P2D2 and Water Hibah). The sole focal legal/governance mechanism is intergovernmental fiscal allocation rules (`institutional_structure_coordination`), specifically output-based performance grants from the Ministry of Finance to local governments (kabupaten and kota). Empirically, the study co-equally evaluates institutional/fiscal intermediate outcomes (`administrative_outcome`: local government capital spending in Tables 3-4 and local government equity investments in municipal water utilities/PDAMs in Tables 5-7) alongside physical household water network hookups (`primary_connection`: log of new household water connections per 1,000 people in Tables 8-10), making `primary_connection` the primary WASH access outcome family and `multiple` the overall outcome label.

This archival historical political ecology study analyzes municipal drinking water governance in colonial Lima (1578-1700) using the Libros de Cabildos de Lima. Multiple governance mechanisms are empirically examined: (1) discretionary evaluation of connection petitions, route adjustments, and free license waivers awarded by Cabildo pipeline commissioners to council insiders, colonial elites, and religious orders (discretion_accommodation, the single most central mechanism reconstructed across Tables 4-6); (2) overlapping municipal public pipelines versus privately funded pipelines subject to public-fountain conditions (regulatory_model_ownership, Table 7); (3) weak compliance enforcement against illegal connections, excess water withdrawals above titled amounts, and convents' non-compliance with public-fountain mandates (enforcement_sanctions); and (4) connection license charges ranging from 100 to 500 pesos alongside selective exemptions (fees_tariffs_subsidies). Outcomes are co-equally focused on sociospatial disparities in household/institutional piped connections and network coverage (primary_connection, primary focal outcome mapped in Figures 3-4) and severe water shortages, service interruptions, and non-functioning public fountains in downstream and Indigenous neighborhoods (effective_access). The study design is an archival qualitative case study combining textual analysis of municipal council minutes with historical cartographic reconstruction.

Full text read (14 pages). Vasquéz and Franceschi (2013) administer a contingent valuation survey of 690 urban households in León, Nicaragua, using a randomized 2x2 split-sample survey experiment ('experimental') that randomly assigns governance provider (centralized national utility ENACAL vs. decentralized municipal provision under Nicaragua's Law of Municipalities Article 7 and National Water Strategy) and water quality level (current vs. safe drinking water), alongside randomized monthly fee bids. The primary mechanism family is 'institutional_structure_coordination' (decentralization of water service mandate from a centralized national utility to municipal government), with 'fees_tariffs_subsidies' secondary as the monthly tariff/cost-recovery payment vehicle. The primary substantive access domain is 'effective_access' (24-hour service reliability/continuity, potability/water quality, and household coping with intermittent supply), while 'assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple' is 'multiple' because the study co-equally estimates household tariff willingness-to-pay and expenditure/income affordability shares ('economic_access') and citizen evaluations of institutional capacity, accountability, local knowledge, and governance preference between ENACAL and the municipality ('administrative_outcome').

This qualitative study (6 focus group discussions with 49 people living with HIV/AIDS and 12 key informant interviews in Mpigi and Gomba districts, Uganda, analyzed via qualitative content analysis) investigates barriers to WASH access among PLWHA. Among rule-type mechanisms, user fees, vendor pricing, and flat-rate tariff structures without pro-poor social tariffs or subsidies at boreholes, water points, and public latrines clearly dominate (`fees_tariffs_subsidies`), alongside secondary mentions of the absence of special institutional accommodations/exemptions (`discretion_accommodation`) and non-participation of PLWHA in water user and sanitary management committees (`participation_assistance`). On the outcome side, both `effective_access` (reliance on contaminated surface-water ponds/lakes, water quality/treatment acceptability, insufficient water quantity, 12 km fetching burden, and physically unsuitable latrines for sick users) and `economic_access` (household inability to afford per-jerrican borehole/vendor fees, per-use public latrine charges, soap, and storage vessels) are co-equally central empirical findings (`multiple`, with `effective_access` as primary).

This case study of Trinidad analyzes residential flat-rate water charges based on the annual rateable value of property (ARV), cost-recovery rules, and implicit subsidies (`fees_tariffs_subsidies`), while secondarily discussing public water utility governance and fiscal autonomy (`regulatory_model_ownership`). Empirically, the paper evaluates multiple co-equal outcome dimensions resulting from this pricing regime (`assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple`: `multiple`), led by widespread service intermittency, rationing, and declining potability (`effective_access`), alongside regressive household expenditure shares (`economic_access`), lack of network expansion in poor settlements (`primary_connection`), and utility revenue shortfalls/unaccounted-for water (`administrative_outcome`). Methodologically, it is a qualitative institutional/policy case study combining review of utility accounts and consultant reports (1988-2008) with key stakeholder and decision-maker interviews conducted in 1993, 2000, 2002, and 2010 (`qualitative`).

This policy and institutional case study examines the implementation of Ecuador's 2008 constitutional human right to water and sanitation. Two governance mechanisms are co-central (`assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple` = `multiple`): (1) `institutional_structure_coordination` (primary), analyzing how SENAGUA fails to operate as a single coordinating water authority amidst overlapping mandates, policies, and uncoordinated public investments across MIDUVI, MAE, MSP, INAR, and 219 municipalities; and (2) `regulatory_model_ownership`, examining constitutional mandates for exclusive public and community management versus ongoing private franchises/concessions (e.g., INTERAGUA in Guayaquil, Amagua in Samborondon, private solid waste services, multilateral privatization programs) and the integration of 9,952 community water systems (JAAPRE), alongside secondary discussion of `participation_assistance` in water governance. On the outcome side (`assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple` = `multiple`), the paper primarily tracks `primary_connection` (national, urban/rural, regional, and socioeconomic trends in residential piped water and public sewer connections from census and survey reports) while also substantially evaluating `effective_access` (service continuity/permanence at 33%, wastewater treatment rates, water quality, and project sustainability). The study design is `qualitative`, synthesizing constitutional/legislative analysis, ministerial management and project evaluation reports (e.g., PRAS), and secondary official descriptive statistics without original statistical modeling.

This secondary case-study synthesis of urban water governance in Ghana centrally examines public-private partnership and ownership/regulatory models (corporatization of GWSC into GWCL, affermage vs. the AVRL management contract, independent regulation by PURC under Act 538, and alternative public-people partnerships), making regulatory_model_ownership the clear primary mechanism (with secondary discussion of structural-adjustment user fees/subsidy removal, urban-rural institutional decoupling, and community self-help participation). On the outcome side, the paper explicitly contrasts wide network coverage and income-stratified household piped hookups (primary_connection) with 'deep access' dimensions of water potability/contamination, intermittency/reliability, and per-capita quantity (effective_access) as well as household affordability and informal tanker price burdens (economic_access), warranting effective_access as primary_outcome_family and multiple for assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple. No primary empirical data are collected; the analysis synthesizes published surveys, reports, and secondary literature (systematic_review_secondary).

Using archival research (legislative files, MALDEF/ACLU legal archives, hearing transcripts, and federal court records), Jepson (2012) conducts a qualitative historical-legal geography case study of two co-central legal mechanisms in South Texas: (1) statutory special-district boundary exclusion/de-annexation and irrigation-versus-domestic mandate demarcation under Texas Article 8280-3.2 (institutional_structure_coordination, primary mechanism), and (2) four years of federal constitutional and Voting Rights Act litigation in Jimenez and Fonseca (review_redress), alongside WCID board electoral participation rules (participation_assistance) and statutory landowner/freeholder candidacy prerequisites and platted/unplatted definitions (eligibility_status_documentation). Because legislative territorial exclusion and federal litigation are co-equally central empirical exposures, assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple is 'multiple'. The primary empirical outcome traced across the archival and judicial record is administrative_outcome—specifically, WCID de-annexation resolutions, ballot refusals, federal court dismissals, WCID conversion into narrow Irrigation Districts, and the institutional/governance foreclosure of colonias residents' political standing to claim treated domestic water.

The paper centrally analyzes cost-reflective pricing, household water metering, tariff differentiation, and inter-regional/inter-household cross-subsidisation in England and Wales (fees_tariffs_subsidies), while situating these pricing reforms within post-1989 privatisation and market environmentalism (regulatory_model_ownership) and examining statutory hosepipe bans during the 2006 drought alongside the UK ban on domestic disconnections (enforcement_sanctions). The focal access outcome is household economic_access—specifically regional disparities in water and sewerage bills and the rising share of low-income households spending over 3% of disposable income on water—evaluated alongside household water demand practices. Empirically, the study employs mixed_methods, combining quantitative secondary statistics from OFWAT/Defra/Environment Agency and a 100-home micro-component water-metering database with qualitative interviews of 22 households and 4 water-company resource teams during the 2006 southeast England drought.

This mixed-methods study (structured questionnaires, key informant interviews, documentation review, narrative and quantitative content analysis, and Chi-squared cross-tabulations across 11 urban local authorities in Zimbabwe) evaluates a multi-pillar bundle of operation and maintenance (O&M) governance arrangements. Multiple rule-based mechanism families are co-equally central empirical components of the scored O&M index: (1) institutional_structure_coordination (statutory mandate allocation between ZINWA and urban councils under the ZINWA Act, Urban Councils Act, and 2012 Water Policy; central-to-local government funding policies; and municipal departmental and decentralized workshop structures, selected as primary), (2) regulatory_model_ownership (municipal department model lacking procurement/financial autonomy, ring-fencing of water accounts, absence of an independent national water regulator, and private-sector maintenance contracting), (3) fees_tariffs_subsidies (cost-recovery and earmarking rules using water tariff revenues for routine and major O&M), and (4) enforcement_sanctions (absence of legally enforceable minimum O&M/service-level standards and penalties under voluntary Service Level Benchmarking). The focal empirical outcomes—functionality of water treatment and conveyancing infrastructure, daily hours of supply continuity, and share of connected properties receiving water regularly—squarely capture effective_access (functional sustainability and service continuity/reliability).

This qualitative study (structured interviews and focus group discussions with 104 purposively sampled women with disabilities plus 7 key informant interviews in three low-income Harare settlements) examines WASH access barriers during the COVID-19 pandemic. The primary rule/governance mechanism analyzed is discretion_accommodation: the failure to implement the National Disability Policy mandate of reasonable accommodation at communal water points, arbitrary and extortionate frontline gatekeeping by community 'borehole marshals' who denied queue priority and demanded cash bribes or transactional sex, and rigid COVID-19 lockdown/curfew and retail sanitiser rules enforced without disability accommodations (with secondary discussion of exclusion from WASH/pandemic planning under participation_assistance and informal water fees/lack of targeted WASH subsidies under fees_tariffs_subsidies). The primary outcome family is effective_access, focusing on physical accessibility of water points, fetching and queueing burdens, water adequacy/quantity for domestic and menstrual hygiene management, and sanitation/hygiene conditions.

This qualitative study (semi-structured interviews with 19 households, 3 community water informants, and 3 national/district officials, plus 2 focus group discussions across three rural Ghanaian communities) examines how decentralized community-based rural water governance operates across five capacity dimensions. Institutional structure and coordination is the overarching primary mechanism (decentralization of mandates and fiscal/training responsibilities from the national Community Water and Sanitation Agency to district assemblies and communities, alongside poor inter-agency coordination and unclear mandate delineation), co-equally analyzed alongside mandated community participation via voluntary Water and Sanitation Committees (including gender quotas) and O&M cost-recovery user fee rules (with secondary discussion of local bylaw and fee payment enforcement gaps), warranting 'multiple' for assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple. On the outcome side, the study primarily evaluates institutional/governance capacity and regulatory compliance outcomes across the five dimensions (e.g., non-compliance with water quality testing and gender composition rules, committee attrition, and uncoordinated data/mandates), while co-centrally documenting severe effective-access failures (frequent hand-pump borehole breakdowns leaving households without potable water for months and reliant on unmonitored streams), warranting 'administrative_outcome' as primary_outcome_family and 'multiple' for assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple.

This qualitative case study of two informal settlements in Xochimilco, Mexico City (using 27 semi-structured key-informant interviews and 41 resident questionnaires transcribed and coded in MAXQDA) examines how legal informality and land-tenure/land-use eligibility rules in the Conservation Zone constrain water supply solutions. Specifically, lack of formal land title and the 2017 Sustainable Water Law prohibit public piped network connections, expanded water-truck delivery, and municipal rainwater-harvesting social programmes in informal settlements (eligibility_status_documentation as the central mechanism, alongside secondary intergovernmental responsibility-shifting between the Alcaldia and SACMEX, informal trucked-water accommodations, and street-level water committees/paradas). Outcomes span effective access (chronic water scarcity, intermittent once- or twice-weekly truck delivery below WHO daily quantity thresholds, and time spent searching for and transporting water), primary piped network connection versus off-grid alternatives, and household economic expenditure on private water purchases, justifying primary_outcome_family = effective_access and assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple = multiple.

This ethnographic and historical legal-anthropological study (1965-2012) examines how statutory law, donor/national project bylaws (CIDA, GWSC, NCWSP), and customary norms interact via institutional bricolage to shape household water access in a Northern Ghana village. Multiple rule-type mechanisms are co-equally central: capital cost-sharing rules (the 5% community contribution), local entrance fees, borehole user fees, and monthly piped-water tariffs (fees_tariffs_subsidies) serve as the primary empirical barrier and focal site of local rule-making, alongside mandated formalization of water user committees and WSDBs (participation_assistance), shifts across private compound wells, centralized state utility management, church ownership, and community management (regulatory_model_ownership), formal membership boundaries tying compounds to single pumps (eligibility_status_documentation), system shutoff/pump removal for tariff non-payment (enforcement_sanctions), and informal customary non-exclusion and poverty fee exemptions (discretion_accommodation). Outcomes are likewise multi-dimensional, centering on source functionality, service continuity, waiting times, fetching distance, and water quantities (effective_access), alongside delivery or non-delivery of boreholes and piped infrastructure (primary_connection), affordability barriers (economic_access), and project application delays/cutoffs (administrative_outcome).

This qualitative study (based on 20 key informant interviews, focus group discussions with gaon samaj leaders, qualitative pipeline mapping, and archival/document review) compares centralized municipal utility provision in Darjeeling with decentralized private for-profit water markets (tankers/handcarts) and community-managed collective systems (gaon samaj). Because the analysis co-equally centers on municipal versus private/community utility ownership and management models (regulatory_model_ownership), decentralized governance, core-periphery jurisdictional/mandate gaps, and lack of municipal-samaj coordination (institutional_structure_coordination), and community water collectives/participatory inclusion (participation_assistance), with secondary discussion of flat municipal water taxes, samaj dues, and tanker pricing (fees_tariffs_subsidies), primary_mechanism_family is regulatory_model_ownership and assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple is multiple. On the outcome side, effective_access (water scarcity/quantity, pipe leakage, alternate-day reliability, potability/contamination, and physical fetching/queuing burdens) is primary alongside co-central analysis of municipal network connection exclusions on the town periphery (primary_connection) and household affordability burdens from expensive tanker water (economic_access), warranting multiple for assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple.

Bakker (2003) is a conceptual political-economy synthesis and typology paper ('other' study design, drawing on descriptive global PPI/WHO statistics and secondary urban case examples) analyzing modes of urban water privatization, concessions, corporatization, and public/private/community ownership models in the global South ('regulatory_model_ownership'). Secondary rule mechanisms discussed include full-cost-recovery tariffs, connection charges, and subsidies ('fees_tariffs_subsidies'), land-tenure and cadastral prerequisites in informal settlements ('eligibility_status_documentation'), and municipal bylaws restricting or charging for private well self-provision ('enforcement_sanctions'). On the outcome side, the paper's central 'archipelago vs network' framing focuses on spatial fragmentation of piped network coverage and household connections ('primary_connection'), while co-equally examining institutional/governance transformations ('administrative_outcome'), tariff affordability ('economic_access'), and service intermittency/quality ('effective_access'), warranting 'multiple' for assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple.

This full-text study is an institutional case study of Cape Verde's water and wastewater sector paired with a normative regulatory design proposal. The central mechanism analyzed is regulatory_model_ownership: the structure and mandate of Cape Verde's independent multi-sector Economic Regulation Agency (ARE, created by Law No. 20/2003), the partial privatization and subsequent re-nationalization of the main utility ELECTRA alongside municipal public utilities, and a proposed sunshine-regulation / yardstick-competition benchmarking model. Secondary mechanisms discussed include increasing-block tariffs, cross-subsidies, and proposed social tariffs (fees_tariffs_subsidies), regulatory compliance monitoring and sanctions (enforcement_sanctions), citizen participation / Water Watch Groups (participation_assistance), and complaint/appeal mechanisms (review_redress), but regulatory_model_ownership clearly dominates. On outcomes, both the descriptive sector diagnosis and the proposed regulatory KPI framework co-equally address service continuity, drinking water potability, and per-capita supply (effective_access), water and sewerage network coverage (primary_connection), tariff affordability (economic_access), and utility operational/complaint/governance metrics (administrative_outcome), justifying effective_access as primary_outcome_family and multiple for assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple. The study relies on documentary legal/regulatory analysis, descriptive secondary utility/national statistics, and an illustrative benchmarking framework rather than statistical inference or primary fieldwork, best fitting qualitative (institutional case study and policy analysis).

Qualitative case study (key-informant interviews, semi-structured interviews with water sellers and users, Blantyre Water Board questionnaires, municipal records, and newspaper content analysis) examining water kiosk governance in Nkolokoti Township, Blantyre, Malawi. The central empirical focus critiques community participation through locally elected water committees (CDCs, water selling committees, and Nkhomano Health and Sanitation Committees; participation_assistance), while co-equally analyzing multi-stakeholder institutional mandates and decentralization failures across the Blantyre City Assembly, Blantyre Water Board, ward councillors, and MPs (institutional_structure_coordination), comparing direct utility-managed vs community-committee-managed kiosk models (regulatory_model_ownership), and examining utility mass disconnections of kiosks for unpaid bill arrears (enforcement_sanctions) alongside kiosk vs private-tap pricing (fees_tariffs_subsidies). Outcomes co-equally center on functional sustainability, continuity, and safe water access for low-income households (effective_access), kiosk governance, revenue arrears, and disconnection incidence (administrative_outcome), and affordability/price burdens when kiosk cutoffs force reliance on higher-priced private taps (economic_access).

This doctrinal legal commentary examines the South African judiciary's adjudication of the constitutional right to water in Lindiwe Mazibuko and Others v City of Johannesburg and Others (High Court, Supreme Court of Appeal and Constitutional Court) concerning the Phiri community in Soweto. Multiple legal and administrative mechanisms are co-equally central: (1) fees_tariffs_subsidies (primary), centering on the adequacy of the 6-kilolitre monthly Free Basic Water allowance, water charges above the free quota, cross-subsidization and Indigent Registration arrears write-offs and 4-kilolitre top-ups; (2) review_redress, analyzing socio-economic rights litigation to compel policy reform and the loss of billing-complaint and pre-disconnection hearing protections under prepaid meters; and (3) enforcement_sanctions, analyzing automatic halting/suspension of supply via prepaid water meters once the free allocation is exhausted (with secondary discussion of eligibility proof, registration paperwork/transport burdens and municipal outreach assistance under the Indigent Persons Policy). Outcomes are likewise multiple: effective_access (primary) focuses on water quantity/sufficiency relative to household size, continuity, reliance on unsafe surface water causing disease and women's fetching burden, alongside co-central economic_access (inability of poor households to afford prepaid water credits and receipt of free/indigent water subsidies) and administrative_outcome (automatic supply cutoffs/suspensions and judicial/policy compliance outcomes).

Full text examined (11 pages). Das and Walton (2015) combine random-sample household survey data (1,200 households across four localities, settlement censuses, and quantitative supplement tables) with multi-year ethnographic interviews and court-record analysis (mixed_methods) to compare struggles over housing and urban infrastructure in two unplanned settlements in Delhi's National Capital Region (Punjabi Basti and NOIDA Sectors 5 and 8). Multiple rule-type mechanisms co-equally structure these struggles: eligibility_status_documentation is the single most pervasive focal mechanism (legal settlement tenure categories, sequential house numbering and an authorized neighborhood map required for metering and colony regularization in Punjabi Basti, and official eligibility surveys, contested beneficiary lists, and ration/voter ID residency documentation in NOIDA), alongside co-central review_redress (civil litigation against Ramjas Foundation and Allahabad High Court stay orders and writ petitions for resettlement), participation_assistance (local political leaders and registered societies navigating bureaucracy), and regulatory_model_ownership / enforcement_sanctions (electricity privatization under BSES and police complaints for electricity theft). The focal empirical outcomes analyzed in the main text are administrative and governance outcomes (administrative_outcome)—official map approval, provisional colony authorization, formal meter regularization, court stay orders against demolition, enumeration on official resettlement lists, and local political leadership structures—while ongoing water and sewage infrastructure projects are noted as open questions rather than evaluated as primary WASH access outcomes in the text.

Prieto (2016) examines the tension between Chile's neoliberal water-rights privatization and market model under the 1981 Water Code and collective indigenous water ownership/customary communal governance (costumbres) among Atacameño communities in Chiu-Chiu and Lasana, making regulatory_model_ownership the dominant mechanism family (with CONADI water-fund purchase subsidies playing a supporting role as fees_tariffs_subsidies). The central empirical outcomes are institutional/governance outcomes (administrative_outcome): water-rights market transaction patterns (only 2 of 213 transactions to mining and 0 to urban utilities) and the recollectivization/decommodification of 58.3% of privatized water volume by indigenous communities while preventing external canal withdrawals. The study uses a mixed_methods design combining a quantitative census of Water Property Register transactions (1981-2009) with three field seasons of participant observation, oral histories, and semi-structured interviews.

This qualitative study (based on ethnographic fieldwork from 2008 to 2017, 30 semi-structured interviews with politicians, administrators, and engineers, and documentary analysis of CAG audits and DJB records) examines multiple co-central legal and governance mechanisms shaping water access in Delhi: (1) institutional_structure_coordination (primary), including Delhi's hybrid city-state intergovernmental oversight structure, Chief Minister political control over the DJB, internal divisions between IAS administrators and engineers, fragmented measurement practices, and blurred jurisdictional boundaries routing water across WTPs, 9 E&M divisions, 22 civil divisions, and assembly constituencies; (2) discretion_accommodation, via street-level bureaucratic arbitrariness and political patronage by MLAs, MCD Councilors, and local DJB engineers who allocate discretionary funds for tankers/tubewells, turn valves, respond selectively to complaints, or overlook illegal tubewells and defunct meters; and (3) eligibility_status_documentation, via Section 9.1.A of the 1998 DJB Act barring formal piped connection rights to informal settlements on unauthorized land. Outcomes span multiple co-central families: effective_access (primary: stark disparities in water quantity in lppd, service intermittency/hours of flow, and unreliable tanker vs piped deliveries), primary_connection (exclusion of informal settlements from central grid connections), and administrative_outcome (institutional illegibility, flawed water/loss accounting, and obscured bureaucratic accountability).

This qualitative public-administration case study analyzes the Sabar Shouchagar ('Toilets for Everyone') initiative in Nadia District, West Bengal, India. Two governance mechanisms are co-equally central (`multiple`): (1) `institutional_structure_coordination`, via multi-agency fiscal and administrative convergence across MGNREGA, NRLM, Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, ICDS, Block Development Officers, and elected Gram Panchayats organized into 6,620 catchment areas; and (2) `participation_assistance`, via CLTS-style community mobilization, women's self-help groups operating 107 rural sanitary marts, NGOs/faith-based groups, and village-level Para Najardari (Neighborhood Monitoring) volunteer committees. Outcomes are likewise co-equally split (`multiple`) between physical household/institutional toilet construction and coverage (`primary_connection`, increasing coverage from 60% to 97% across 336,000+ families) and sustained functional toilet adoption/elimination of open defecation (`effective_access`, increasing usage from 57% to 99.8%).

This full-text paper conducts an ex-ante Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) using Multiple Criteria Decision Analysis (M-MACBETH), stakeholder focus-group/survey elicitation, and cost-benefit analysis for the state water/wastewater regulator of Minas Gerais (ARSAE) across four municipalities (Belo Horizonte, Betim, Contagem, and Ribeirao das Neves). Because ARSAE lacks municipal legal authority to inspect households or directly enforce mandatory sewer connection statutes, its primary actionable and quantitatively modeled regulatory lever is tariff and cost-recovery/subsidy design (CEc1: average tariffs covering capex/opex to finance connection diffusion while addressing user resistance to higher tariffs), making fees_tariffs_subsidies the dominant primary mechanism alongside contextual discussion of mandatory-connection enforcement (enforcement_sanctions), state-regulator vs municipal mandate division (institutional_structure_coordination), and independent regulatory agency governance via RIA (regulatory_model_ownership). The focal access outcome evaluated across the four policy alternatives (100%, 75%, 50%, and 0% gap reduction) is physical household connection to the public wastewater network (CSo1: number of non-connected households), classified as primary_connection. Because the empirical exercise evaluates hypothetical prospective policy scenarios via ex-ante MCDA and cost-benefit decision modeling rather than observing post-intervention outcomes, study_design_class is classified as other.

This mixed-methods case study of Mebane, North Carolina combines GIS spatial analysis of 2000 Census demographic data and geocoded sewer/zoning records with participant observation and content analysis of town council deliberations. Its central legal-institutional mechanism is municipal underbounding—specifically the strategic drawing of municipal corporate limits, selective annexation, and Extra-Territorial Jurisdiction (ETJ) boundary governance (`institutional_structure_coordination`), reinforced by selective local official discretion in land-use/watershed overlays (`discretion_accommodation`)—used to exclude historic African American neighborhoods from the city limits and thereby deny them municipal sewer line extensions (`primary_connection`).

This qualitative study (40 key informant interviews and focus group discussions across six iTaukei villages in Fiji, analyzed thematically) examines village-level water committees—a formal requirement to access support under the Water Authority of Fiji Rural Water Scheme—focusing on committee membership rules, user/gender participation, and polycentric coordination across household, committee, village, and district/provincial levels (primary mechanism: participation_assistance). The central empirical outcomes analyzed across the four results themes are institutional and governance intermediate outcomes (committee structures, reporting and accountability mechanisms, village/committee decision-making processes, gendered member roles, and proactive vs. reactive maintenance routines), placing the primary outcome in administrative_outcome.

This qualitative ethnographic and policy case study (based on archival research, 18 formal semi-structured interviews, and participant observation in 2010-2011) examines indigenous water justice in the Mataranka (Tindal Aquifer) Water Allocation Plan in Australia's Northern Territory. Using Fraser's tripartite justice framework, the study co-equally analyzes participatory water planning mechanisms and advisory committees (statutory Water Advisory Committees under NT water law, National Water Initiative participatory planning mandates, and the NLC-established Mataranka Traditional Owner Water Allocation Reference Group: participation_assistance), formal entitlement and native-title eligibility rules governing the Strategic Indigenous Reserve (comparing the Katherine Plan's native-title proof prerequisite against the Mataranka Plan's unconditional 25% commercial reserve: eligibility_status_documentation), and jurisdictional boundaries and statutory-customary governance coordination (boundedness of the Water Control District, narrow agency mandates excluding riparian vegetation, and articulation with local indigenous governance: institutional_structure_coordination). Because participatory planning representation and formal reserve/native-title entitlement rules are co-equally central empirical foci, primary_mechanism_family is participation_assistance and assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple is multiple. Evaluated outcomes center on governance and regulatory planning intermediate outcomes (allocated commercial reserve shares and their deferral, formal plan recognition of indigenous cultural values, and stakeholder representation legitimacy: administrative_outcome).

Ethnographic qualitative study (participant-observation, semistructured interviews in 18 households, community meetings, and key-informant interviews with officials and growers) in Baja California's San Quintin Valley. Among legal and regulatory mechanisms affecting domestic water access, fees_tariffs_subsidies clearly dominates: the analysis contrasts state desalination, electricity, and well-meter subsidies for export agribusinesses under CNA with full cost-recovery policies enforced on colonia residents by the state urban utility CESPE (proposed 300% and enacted 115% flat-rate tariff increases, unsubsidized $227 household meter fees, three-part connection/piping/meter charges, and priced barrel quotas), alongside secondary discussions of decentralized agency mandates under the 1992 National Water Law (institutional_structure_coordination), weak CNA enforcement against unpermitted agricultural wells (enforcement_sanctions), and captured watershed councils/COTAS (participation_assistance). Outcomes are co-equally multi-dimensional (multiple), centered on effective_access (declining water quantity and quality from salinity and unfiltered muddy tap water, severe service intermittency, and barrel rationing) alongside economic_access (farmworker households spending ~14% of income on trucked water, tariff burden, and unaffordable meter charges) and primary_connection (40% of colonias lacking piped running water).

Zerah (2008) conducts a qualitative historical-institutional case study of Mumbai's water/sanitation and electricity sectors (supplemented by descriptive Census 2001 tabulations and secondary utility benchmarks) to test the splintering urbanism thesis. Multiple legal-institutional mechanisms are co-equally central empirical exposures: utility ownership and regulatory governance reforms (`regulatory_model_ownership`, including municipal monopoly vs private licensing, unbundling, corporatisation, ward-level delegated management contracts, and independent regulation) serve as the overarching analytical frame alongside tariff, ring-fenced cost-recovery, connection-fee, and cross-subsidy rules (`fees_tariffs_subsidies`), land-tenure and slum-notification service entitlements (`eligibility_status_documentation`), mandated CBO financial and operational participation in the Slum Sanitation Program (`participation_assistance`), complex connection procedures and mandatory licensed plumbers (`procedural_burden`), and metropolitan jurisdictional fragmentation (`institutional_structure_coordination`). Outcomes span household tap/sewerage/latrine network coverage (`primary_connection`, the primary water/sanitation metric in Table 2 and Section 3.2.1) alongside service intermittency, per-capita quantity, and shared vs in-premise service differentiation (`effective_access`) and household connection/tariff affordability (`economic_access`), warranting `multiple` for the multi-label outcome field.

This quasi-experimental study uses municipal panel difference-in-differences models (with municipality and year fixed effects and propensity-score common-support trimming) across Colombian municipalities (1990-2005) to evaluate the 1994 Law 142 utility reforms enacted within Colombia's 1990s municipal decentralization framework. The central empirical exposure (regulatory_model_ownership) compares corporatized specialized providers (government-owned EICEs and public, mixed, or private ESP S.A. utility corporations, including interactions for private/mixed capital participation) against continued direct municipal provision, while decentralization (institutional_structure_coordination) forms the enabling institutional background allowing local governments to choose whether to reform. Alongside child mortality, the water/sanitation access outcome empirically estimated is municipal household water supply and sewerage coverage from the 1993 and 2005 censuses (primary_connection).

This qualitative desktop and key-informant interview/observation study (conducted across six urban councils and ZINWA from 2008 to 2012) diagnoses the causes and impacts of urban domestic water and sanitation failures in Zimbabwe. Among legal and governance mechanisms, the central empirical bottleneck analyzed is intergovernmental centralization and lack of municipal fiscal/operational autonomy (`institutional_structure_coordination`): urban councils depend on central government for capital infrastructure funding, must obtain central government approval for major projects, parts procurement, and tariff adjustments, and share fragmented responsibilities with ZINWA. Cost-recovery tariff constraints and metering/pricing rules (`fees_tariffs_subsidies`) and weak statutory pollution fines alongside municipal payment-default water disconnections (`enforcement_sanctions`) are secondary applicable mechanisms. The primary outcome analyzed throughout is `effective_access`—specifically severe service intermittency, daily/prolonged water rationing, declining water quantity and potability, collapsed sewage reticulation, reliance on unsafe shallow wells, and resulting water-borne disease outbreaks.

This qualitative study (38 semi-structured interviews, participant observation, participatory mapping, and a focus group with Lilongwe Water Board staff) examines how uncodified street-level bureaucratic discretion, ad hoc valve manipulation, case-by-case backup-line diversions, high-pressure bypass connections for influential clients, and differentiated maintenance responses by utility engineers and operators (`discretion_accommodation`) produce socio-spatial inequalities in water supply continuity, pressure, and service hours across low-income versus high-income areas within Lilongwe's piped network (`effective_access`).

Acey (2010) uses a mixed-methods design combining 783 household surveys across 18 neighbourhoods in Lagos and Benin City with qualitative semi-structured interviews to analyze gendered community mobilisation and Hirschman's exit, voice, and loyalty responses to urban water supply failures. Multiple institutional mechanisms are co-central: community participation and mobilisation through voluntary associations such as Community Development Associations, landlord/tenant associations, and religious groups (participation_assistance, primary mechanism frame) alongside official consumer complaint/grievance channels to utilities and government ministries (review_redress), complicated by property-owner/receipt prerequisites for complaining to the Lagos Water Corporation (eligibility_status_documentation) and accountability gaps from informal private water vending competing with public utilities (regulatory_model_ownership). Empirically measured outcomes span both civic complaint/governance engagement and inability to influence sector decision-making (administrative_outcome, focal dependent variable) as well as household service intermittency, daily water quantity, potability, fetching burden (effective_access), and high vendor water expenditure (economic_access).

This mixed-methods binational comparative study (combining a 2016 survey of 152 households compared against a 1996 baseline survey, 60 semistructured interviews, and participant observation) examines how Palomas, Chihuahua, and Columbus, New Mexico, addressed arsenic- and fluoride-contaminated groundwater from the shared Mimbres Basin Aquifer. Multiple legal and institutional mechanisms are co-equally analyzed: (1) institutional_structure_coordination is the overarching comparative exposure (asymmetric U.S. vs. Mexican national/binational water governance and funding, official U.S. colonia designation unlocking federal/state grants vs. Mexico's 1992 Water Law decentralizing utilities and cutting federal subsidies); (2) fees_tariffs_subsidies (utility full cost-recovery mandates in Mexico preventing centralized RO filtration and pricing kiosk water at US$0.25/5 gal, alongside 200-300% water/sewer/landfill bill increases in Columbus to finance RO/wastewater loans and membrane replacement); and (3) enforcement_sanctions (an EPA Safe Drinking Water Act administrative order forcing Columbus to adopt expensive centralized RO rather than cheaper adsorbents, plus property liens and ~10% household disconnections for nonpayment), with secondary discussion of informal bill negotiation (discretion_accommodation) and marginalization in rate hearings (participation_assistance). On the outcome side, multiple outcome families are co-equally central ('Potable or Affordable?'): effective_access (primary focus on arsenic/fluoride potability, service reliability, perceived waterborne illness, and physical hauling access to decentralized RO kiosks), economic_access (household water expenditure share rising to 4.9% of income in Columbus and 7.7% in Palomas, exceeding the 2.5% EPA affordability benchmark), primary_connection (centralized network connection reaching 100% by 2016), and administrative_outcome (utility disconnections for delinquency in Columbus).

This cross-national panel study (31 Sub-Saharan African countries, 1990-2005, N=70 country-year observations) uses two-way fixed effects OLS and instrumental-variable regressions to test the effect of aggregate per-capita IMF structural adjustment loan amounts on infant mortality rates. Although the narrative background mentions subsidy cuts, health/education user fees, and asset privatization among broad macroeconomic structural adjustment conditionalities, no water or sanitation legal/regulatory rule-type mechanism is empirically operationalized or tested (NONE_NO_RULE_MECHANISM). Likewise, the sole dependent variable across all models in Tables 1 and 2 is infant mortality (a health outcome), while national access to an improved water and sanitation source enters only as a right-hand-side independent/mediating covariate rather than an analyzed access outcome (NONE_NO_ACCESS_OUTCOME). The longitudinal country-panel regression design using secondary macro indicators is observational.

Birkenholtz (2010) examines Jaipur's Asian Development Bank-backed water-supply reforms, centering primarily on full-cost-recovery pricing, connection fees, and rising-block tariffs (fees_tariffs_subsidies) alongside co-central public-private partnership restructuring (regulatory_model_ownership), incomplete decentralization and overlapping mandates between Urban Local Bodies and the state PHED under the 74th Constitutional Amendment (institutional_structure_coordination), and legal service mandates tied to slum regularization status (eligibility_status_documentation). Using a 2007 stratified household survey across six neighborhoods (reporting quantitative water availability and monthly household water expenditures in Table 2) combined with 2007 and 2009 qualitative interviews with households, PHED engineers, and tanker operators (mixed_methods), the paper evaluates both service intermittency, water quality, queuing/fetching burdens, and adaptive self-provisioning (effective_access) and class-stratified monthly household water expenditures and cost burdens (economic_access), as well as household versus standpost connection type (primary_connection) and utility cost-recovery deficits (administrative_outcome).

Based on 22 months of ethnographic fieldwork in Mumbai (qualitative design), Anand (2012) examines how Muslim residents in Premnagar—despite many holding pre-1995 recognized settlement status—are disconnected from reliable municipal water through street-level bureaucratic discretion and informal workarounds (discretion_accommodation). Municipal water engineers selectively neglect maintenance, judge complainants' legitimacy, and gatekeep complaints behind paid-bill proofs, while licensed/informal plumbers mediate access through unauthorized connections and negotiated compromises. Secondary rule mechanisms discussed include formal documentation/ID and licensed-plumber requirements and arduous billing/complaint steps (procedural_burden, eligibility_status_documentation, review_redress), estimated billing without subsidies (fees_tariffs_subsidies), and periodic raids/cutoffs of unauthorized pipes (enforcement_sanctions). Outcomes span co-equally central dimensions (multiple), led by effective_access (rusted/dry mains, low pressure, 4:30 AM collection schedules, gendered fetching burdens, and reliance on sewage-contaminated unpotable borewells) alongside primary_connection (shift from formal municipal hookups to unauthorized plumber connections and borewell networks), administrative_outcome (refusal/delay of complaints and applications), and economic_access (high repeated connection payments to plumbers and estimated bills for dry lines).

Full-text empirical paper evaluating Shelter Associates' 'One Home-One Toilet' (OHOT) urban slum sanitation model across four cities in Maharashtra (463 households surveyed pre- and post-intervention, six months apart). The intervention combines two co-central rule/delivery mechanisms: (1) NGO-led community mobilization, GIS mapping/ULB coordination, and women's sanitation committees (`participation_assistance`, primary framing mechanism), and (2) an explicit cost-sharing subsidy rule in which the NGO supplies construction materials in phases while beneficiary households bear labour and finishing costs (`fees_tariffs_subsidies`, empirically evaluated in Section 3). Outcomes span functional toilet usage replacing Community Toilet Blocks/open defecation and >6-month functionality (`effective_access`, primary pre-post outcome), physical household toilet installation inside small slum dwellings (`primary_connection`), and household cost-sharing expenditure (`economic_access`). The primary dataset analyzed in Tables 1-4 is an observational single-group pre-post household survey of 463 beneficiary families.

This cross-sectional observational study surveys 160 households across 16 randomly selected rural water supply systems in Achefer, Ethiopia, using Tobit censored regressions to test determinants of household management contributions. The central institutional mechanisms tested as explanatory exposures belong to participation_assistance: degree of household participation during project design and implementation (DPARDPIMP), trust in village water use committees (TOWUCs), and project health/management advocacy (ADVOCACY), alongside contextual discussion of WUC-set monthly tariffs/cost-recovery rules (fees_tariffs_subsidies). The empirical dependent variables are household cash contributions (CASHCONT) and labour contributions (LABORCONT) toward WUC operation and maintenance (plus aggregate O&M cost-coverage adequacy at 19%), which represent institutional/governance intermediate and contribution-compliance outcomes (administrative_outcome) rather than direct empirical outcomes of physical connection or service functionality.
